5-1.bio:
The Holy Prophet Jeremiah lived in Jerusalem in the seventh and sixth centuries before Christ. Called by God from his youth, he warned the people of Judah of the coming destruction of the city for their unfaithfulness, and wept over its fall in his Lamentations. His words were often rejected, and he suffered imprisonment for speaking the truth; tradition holds that he ended his life in Egypt.

The Church honors him among the four great prophets, for his prophecies of the new covenant God would write upon the hearts of His people point to Christ. He is commemorated on May 1.
5-1.name: Jeremiah the Prophet

5-1.bio:
Euthymios of the Peloponnese, Ignatios of Stara Zagora and Akakios of Neochori near Thessaloniki were three young men who had denied Christ under pressure and later repented. Each prepared for confession under the guidance of the elders of the Skete of the Forerunner (Iviron) on Mount Athos.

One after another they went to Constantinople and confessed their faith openly, and were beheaded there between 1814 and 1816. Their relics were brought back to the Holy Mountain, where the three are honored together on May 1.
5-1.desc: Synaxis of the three Athonite New Martyrs Euthymios, Ignatios and Akakios, who suffered in Constantinople in the early nineteenth century.
5-1.name: Akakios, Euthymios and Ignatios the New Martyrs of Athos

5-1.bio:
Isidora was a nun of the women's monastery of Tabennisi in Egypt in the fourth century. She took the lowliest tasks of the kitchen, ate only scraps, and let the sisters mock her as a simpleton, bearing everything without complaint.

Tradition relates that the hermit Pitirim was shown by an angel that this despised sister surpassed him in virtue; when he came and bowed before her, the sisters repented of their contempt. Unable to endure their honor, Isidora quietly left the monastery and ended her life in obscurity.
5-1.desc: Venerable Isidora of Tabennisi in Egypt, who hid her holiness beneath the appearance of folly.
5-1.name: Isidora the Fool-for-Christ

5-1.bio:
Tamara reigned over Georgia from 1184 until her death in 1213, a period remembered as the golden age of the Georgian kingdom. She was known for her humility, her justice toward the poor, and her generous support of churches, monasteries and the Georgian houses on Mount Athos and in the Holy Land.

The Georgian Church honors her as a holy ruler; her feast is kept on May 1 and again on the Sunday of the Myrrhbearers.
5-1.desc: Holy Queen Tamara of Georgia, pious ruler and patron of churches and monasteries.
5-1.name: Tamara the Queen of Georgia

5-1.bio:
Panaretos served as Archbishop of Paphos in Cyprus during the eighteenth century, when the island lay under Ottoman rule. Though a bishop, he kept the strict fasting and prayer of a monk, slept on the ground, and gave what he had to the poor.

Tradition relates that he was granted the gift of insight and worked healings during his lifetime. He reposed in peace in 1791 and is venerated especially in Paphos.
5-1.desc: Saint Panaretos, Archbishop of Paphos in Cyprus, an ascetic bishop of the eighteenth century.
5-1.name: Panaretos of Paphos

5-1.bio:
Nikephoros was born on Chios in the eighteenth century and became a monk at the Nea Moni of the island. A learned man, he taught in the school of Chios and was a close friend of Saint Athanasios of Paros and Saint Makarios of Corinth, sharing their zeal for the frequent reception of Holy Communion and the Church's traditions.

He composed services and lives of saints, including of the New Martyrs, and reposed in peace on Chios in 1821.
5-1.desc: Venerable Nikephoros of Chios, monk, teacher and hymnographer of the Kollyvades tradition.
5-1.name: Nikephoros of Chios

5-1.bio:
Maria, called Methymopoula, was a young Christian woman of the village of Fourni in eastern Crete. Tradition relates that she was pursued by a Turkish official and, refusing to abandon her faith and her chastity, was killed in 1826.

She is honored as a New Martyr of Crete, and the village of Fourni keeps her memory on May 1.
5-1.desc: New Martyr Maria the Methymopoula of Fourni in Crete, a virgin who died for her faith under Ottoman rule.
5-1.name: Maria of Fourni

5-10.bio:
The Holy Apostle Simon the Zealot was one of the Twelve chosen by the Lord. The Gospels record his name among the Apostles, and his title of Zealot bespeaks his burning devotion. After Pentecost he went forth like the others to preach the Gospel, and tradition holds that he carried the good news to distant lands and completed his course as a martyr.

Though the synaxaria preserve few details of his labors, the Church honors him as one of the foundation stones of apostolic preaching. He is commemorated on May 10.
5-10.name: Simon the Zealot

5-10.bio:
Alphaeus, Philadelphus and Cyprinus were brothers, sons of a nobleman of southern Italy, who were arrested for their faith in the third century and taken through several cities before reaching Leontini in Sicily.

There, after refusing to sacrifice, they were put to death by various means. They are honored as patrons of Leontini.
5-10.desc: Holy Martyrs Alphaeus, Philadelphus and Cyprinus, three brothers who suffered in Sicily.
5-10.name: Alphaeus, Philadelphus and Cyprinus

5-10.bio:
Hesychios was a high-ranking official in Antioch in the reign of Maximian Galerius. When Christians were ordered to leave the imperial service, he willingly laid aside his rank, and when he refused to sacrifice he was thrown into the river Orontes with a millstone about his neck.

He is commemorated on May 10.
5-10.desc: Holy Martyr Hesychios of Antioch, a senior official drowned in the Orontes for his faith.
5-10.name: Hesychios of Antioch

5-10.bio:
Erasmus and Onesimus, with fourteen companions, are remembered together with the brothers Alphaeus, Philadelphus and Cyprinus as martyrs of Sicily. They were converted through the witness of the three brothers and shared their confession and death.

They are commemorated on May 10.
5-10.desc: Holy Martyrs Erasmus, Onesimus and the fourteen who suffered with them in Sicily.
5-10.name: Erasmus and Onesimus with Fourteen Martyrs

5-10.bio:
The synaxarion records Venerable Laurence as a monk who lived a life of asceticism and reposed in peace. Some accounts place him in the monasteries near Constantinople.

He is commemorated on May 10.
5-10.desc: Venerable Laurence, a monk who reposed in peace.
5-10.name: Laurence the Monk

5-10.bio:
Passarion was a priest and archimandrite in Jerusalem in the fifth century, remembered for building a hospice for the poor and a monastery on Mount Sion. The monks Agapios and Philemon are honored with him.

They reposed in peace and are commemorated on May 10.
5-10.desc: Venerable Passarion the Presbyter, with Agapios and Philemon, ascetics of Palestine.
5-10.name: Passarion, Agapios and Philemon

5-11.bio:
The Holy Hieromartyr Mocius was a priest who suffered for Christ at the beginning of the fourth century, during the persecution of Diocletian. Preaching boldly against the worship of idols, he was arrested and endured many torments, and was finally beheaded at Byzantium, faithful to the end.

He was venerated in that city from early times, and St. Constantine the Great raised a great church in his honor in the new capital. His feast on May 11 coincides with the day Constantinople was dedicated, and he is remembered as one of the city's heavenly protectors.
5-11.desc: Hieromartyr Mocius, patron of the founding of Constantinople.
5-11.name: Mocius the Martyr

5-11.bio:
Cyril (baptized Constantine) and his elder brother Methodios were born in Thessalonica in the ninth century. Sent by the Emperor and Patriarch Photios to Moravia, they devised an alphabet for the Slavonic language and translated the Scriptures and services, so that the Slavs might worship in their own tongue.

Cyril died in Rome in 869 and Methodios, as Archbishop of Moravia, continued the work until his repose in 885. Their disciples carried the Slavonic liturgy to Bulgaria and beyond.
5-11.desc: Saints Cyril and Methodios of Thessalonica, Equals-to-the-Apostles and enlighteners of the Slavic peoples.
5-11.name: Cyril and Methodios, Enlighteners of the Slavs

5-11.bio:
On May 11 in the year 330 the Emperor Constantine formally dedicated the city of Byzantium as the new capital of the empire, placing it under the protection of the Theotokos. The city became the seat of the Ecumenical Patriarchate and the heart of the Orthodox world.

The Church has kept the anniversary of the dedication each year.
5-11.desc: Commemoration of the dedication of Constantinople as the New Rome by Saint Constantine the Great.
5-11.name: Founding of Constantinople

5-11.bio:
Argyrios was born in Epanomi near Thessalonica in the late eighteenth century and worked as a tailor in the city. When a Christian who had apostatized was being taken to be judged, Argyrios openly urged him to return to Christ, and was himself arrested.

Refusing all pressure to embrace Islam, he was hanged in Thessalonica in 1806 at the age of about eighteen.
5-11.desc: New Martyr Argyrios of Epanomi, a young tailor hanged at Thessalonica for confessing Christ.
5-11.name: Argyrios of Epanomi

5-11.bio:
Olympia was born in Constantinople and became a nun on the island of Lesbos, where she was joined by Euphrosyne. Tradition relates that pirates raided their monastery in the thirteenth century and, when the nuns refused to renounce Christ, put Olympia to death with nails.

Their relics were later found and are venerated on Lesbos.
5-11.desc: Venerable Martyrs Olympia and Euphrosyne, nuns of Mytilene slain by invaders.
5-11.name: Olympia and Euphrosyne of Mytilene

5-11.bio:
Dioskoros was a Christian who confessed his faith before the Turkish authorities and, refusing to convert, was put to death, tradition placing his martyrdom at Smyrna. Few details of his life are preserved.

He is commemorated on May 11.
5-11.desc: New Martyr Dioskoros, who suffered at Smyrna.
5-11.name: Dioskoros the New

5-12.bio:
The Holy Martyr Modestos suffered for Christ in the early centuries of the Church. Of his life the synaxaria preserve little beyond his faithful confession, that he refused to deny the Lord and sealed his witness with his blood.

The Church keeps his memory among the countless martyrs whose names are written in heaven, honoring in him the victory of faith over the fear of death. He is commemorated on May 12.
5-12.name: Modestos

5-12.bio:
Epiphanios was born in Palestine of Jewish parents in the early fourth century and came to Christ as a young man. He became a monk under Saint Hilarion and founded a monastery near Eleutheropolis before being chosen bishop of Salamis in Cyprus in 367.

He was a tireless defender of Orthodox teaching, author of the Panarion against the heresies, and was loved for his generosity to the poor. He reposed at sea in 403 while returning from Constantinople.
5-12.desc: Saint Epiphanios, Bishop of Salamis (Constantia) and Archbishop of Cyprus, champion of the faith.
5-12.name: Epiphanios of Cyprus

5-12.bio:
Germanos was born in Constantinople in the seventh century, son of a patrician executed by the emperor. Raised among the clergy of the Great Church, he became Bishop of Cyzicus and in 715 Patriarch of Constantinople.

When Leo the Isaurian began his attack on the holy icons, Germanos refused to sign the decree and resigned his throne in 730. He lived out his days in retirement and reposed around 740; his hymns are still sung in the Church.
5-12.desc: Saint Germanos, Patriarch of Constantinople, confessor for the holy icons.
5-12.name: Germanos of Constantinople

5-12.bio:
Theodore was born in Koroni in the Peloponnese and, after serving as a cleric, left his family for the ascetic life. He withdrew to the then-deserted island of Kythera, where he lived alone in prayer and hardship.

He reposed there in the tenth century, and his relics and church remain the spiritual center of the island.
5-12.desc: Venerable Theodore, the hermit of Kythera.
5-12.name: Theodore of Kythera

5-12.bio:
John was born in Oltenia in Wallachia in the seventeenth century and was taken captive by the Turks as a young man. Brought to Constantinople, he was repeatedly pressured to accept Islam and to yield to his captor's immoral demands.

He refused steadfastly and was hanged in 1662. He is honored by the Romanian and Greek Churches.
5-12.desc: New Martyr John of Wallachia, a Romanian youth strangled in Constantinople for refusing Islam.
5-12.name: John of Wallachia

5-12.bio:
Pancratius was born in Phrygia and brought to Rome as an orphan by his uncle, where both were baptized. During the persecution of Diocletian the boy, only about fourteen years old, refused to sacrifice to the gods and was beheaded on the Via Aurelia around the year 304.

A basilica was raised over his tomb in Rome.
5-12.desc: Holy Martyr Pancratius, a boy of fourteen beheaded at Rome.
5-12.name: Pancratius of Rome

5-12.bio:
Hermogenes was Metropolitan of Kazan before being chosen Patriarch of Moscow in 1606 during the Time of Troubles. When Polish forces occupied Moscow, he refused to endorse the foreign claimant and sent letters calling the Russian people to rise in defense of Orthodoxy.

Imprisoned in the Chudov Monastery, he was starved to death in 1612. He was glorified in 1913.
5-12.desc: Hieromartyr Hermogenes, Patriarch of Moscow, who died in prison for the faith and the Russian land.
5-12.name: Hermogenes of Moscow

5-13.bio:
The Holy Martyr Glykeria was a young Christian woman of Thrace who suffered for Christ in the second century. The daughter of a Roman official, she confessed the Lord openly when the pagans of Heraclea gathered for sacrifice, refusing to honor the idols. For this she endured imprisonment and many tortures, and was finally given over to wild beasts, ending her contest with prayer.

Her name means sweetness, and the Church remembers in her the sweetness of a soul wholly given to Christ. She is commemorated on May 13.
5-13.name: Glykeria

5-13.bio:
Sergios was a nobleman of Constantinople, related to Patriarch Photios, who lived during the second period of Iconoclasm in the ninth century. For his defense of the icons he was stripped of his property and exiled with his family.

He endured his sufferings with patience and reposed in peace after the restoration of the icons.
5-13.desc: Venerable Sergios the Confessor, who suffered exile for the holy icons.
5-13.name: Sergios the Confessor

5-13.bio:
John, a Georgian nobleman, and his son Euthymios came to Mount Athos in the tenth century and, with the support of Saint Athanasios of the Lavra, founded the Monastery of the Iberians. Euthymios translated the Scriptures and Fathers into Georgian, and George the Hagiorite later continued the work as abbot.

The monk Gabriel is remembered for receiving the icon of the Panagia Portaitissa from the sea. The four are honored together on May 13.
5-13.desc: Venerable John, Euthymios, George and Gabriel the Iberians, founders and fathers of the Iviron Monastery on Mount Athos.
5-13.greek: Ιωάννης, Ευθύμιος, Γεώργιος και Γαβριήλ οι Ίβηρες
5-13.name: Founders of Iviron: John, Euthymios, George and Gabriel

5-13.bio:
Laodikios was the guard of the prison where the virgin martyr Glykeria was held at Heraclea in Thrace. Witnessing her endurance and the wonders that accompanied her sufferings, he confessed Christ himself.

He was beheaded and is honored with her on May 13.
5-13.desc: Holy Martyr Laodikios, the jailer converted by Saint Glykeria.
5-13.name: Laodikios the Jailer

5-13.bio:
Pausikakos was born in Apamea in Syria and practiced medicine, healing the sick freely and treating souls as well as bodies. Chosen Bishop of Synnada in Phrygia in the sixth century, he was loved for his charity.

Tradition relates that he healed the Emperor Maurice and that he reposed in peace around the year 606.
5-13.desc: Saint Pausikakos, Bishop of Synnada, physician and wonderworker.
5-13.name: Pausikakos of Synnada

5-13.bio:
In the late thirteenth century, when the Emperor Michael VIII sought to impose the union with Rome, the monks of Iviron on Mount Athos refused to accept it. Tradition relates that the elder monks were put aboard a ship and drowned in the sea, while the younger were carried off into captivity.

They are honored among the Athonite martyrs for Orthodoxy.
5-13.desc: Holy Monastic Martyrs of the Iviron Monastery, drowned for refusing the Latin union.
5-13.name: Monastic Martyrs of Iviron

5-14.bio:
The Holy Martyr Isidore suffered on the island of Chios in the middle of the third century, during the persecution of Decius. A soldier serving in the imperial fleet, he was denounced as a Christian, and when he refused to sacrifice to the idols he was tortured and beheaded, remaining steadfast in his confession to the end.

He has been venerated on Chios from ancient times as the island's own martyr, and churches in his honor spread from there throughout the Christian world. He is commemorated on May 14.
5-14.name: Isidore of Chios

5-14.bio:
Therapon was a bishop in Cyprus who suffered martyrdom for Christ; the details of his life are not preserved. His relics remained on the island until the ninth century, when, tradition relates, the saint appeared and directed that they be moved to Constantinople before an Arab raid.

Many healings were attributed to his relics in the capital.
5-14.desc: Hieromartyr Therapon, Bishop in Cyprus, whose relics were brought to Constantinople.
5-14.name: Therapon of Cyprus

5-14.bio:
Leontios was born in Stroumitsa in Macedonia and became a monk of the Monastery of Saint John on Patmos, later serving as its abbot. In the twelfth century he was chosen Patriarch of Jerusalem and journeyed to the Holy Land, where the Crusaders prevented him from taking possession of his see.

He returned to Constantinople, where he reposed in 1185, renowned for wonders and for his gift of clairvoyance.
5-14.desc: Saint Leontios, Patriarch of Jerusalem, former abbot of Patmos.
5-14.name: Leontios of Jerusalem

5-14.bio:
Mark was a Cretan who had denied Christ in his youth and lived as a Muslim in Smyrna. Stricken with remorse, he confessed his return to Christ before the judge and refused every inducement to recant.

He was beheaded in Smyrna in 1643.
5-14.desc: New Martyr Mark of Crete, beheaded at Smyrna.
5-14.name: Mark of Crete

5-14.bio:
John was a young goldsmith from Bulgaria who worked in Constantinople. Falsely accused and pressured to accept Islam, he confessed Christ openly before the court.

He was beheaded in 1802.
5-14.desc: New Martyr John the Bulgarian, a goldsmith beheaded in Constantinople.
5-14.name: John the Bulgarian

5-14.bio:
The synaxarion honors the martyrs Aristotle and Leander on May 14, recording that they gave their lives for Christ. The place and time of their martyrdom are not preserved.

They are commemorated together with the Martyr Isidore of Chios.
5-14.name: Aristotle and Leander

5-15.bio:
St. Pachomios the Great was born in Egypt at the end of the third century. A pagan conscript soldier, he was won to Christ by the kindness of Christians to the troops, and after baptism took up the ascetic life in the desert. At Tabennisi by the Nile he founded the first great communities of monks living a common life under a rule, and thousands gathered under his guidance.

With St. Anthony he stands at the head of Egyptian monasticism, the father of the cenobitic way that spread through the whole Church. He reposed in the fourth century and is commemorated on May 15.
5-15.desc: Founder of communal monasticism in Egypt.
5-15.name: Pachomios the Great

5-15.bio:
Achillios was born in Cappadocia and, after travels in the Holy Land and Rome, was chosen Bishop of Larisa in Thessaly in the fourth century. He took part in the Council of Nicaea in 325, where tradition relates that he confounded the Arians by a miracle.

He built churches, destroyed pagan temples and worked many wonders, reposing around 330. His relics were carried to Prespa in the tenth century and returned to Larisa in 1981.
5-15.desc: Saint Achillios, Bishop of Larisa, wonderworker and father of the First Ecumenical Council.
5-15.name: Achillios of Larisa

5-15.bio:
Barbaros was a North African who came to Greece with pirates and lived as a brigand in the region of Aetolia. Moved to repentance, tradition relates, he confessed to a priest and spent years in penance in the wilderness, walking on all fours as a beast.

He was killed by hunters who mistook him for an animal, and after his death fragrant myrrh flowed from his body. He is honored in Aetolia and Epirus.
5-15.desc: Venerable Barbaros the Myrrhstreamer, the former robber who became an ascetic in Aetolia.
5-15.name: Barbaros the Myrrhstreamer

5-15.bio:
Andrew was born in Monodendri in Epirus and lived as a hermit in a cave near Kalana in the mountains of Aetolia, tradition placing him in the thirteenth century. He spent his life in prayer and hardship and was known for the wonders worked through him.

His cave and relics remain a place of pilgrimage.
5-15.desc: Venerable Andrew the Hermit and Wonderworker of Epirus.
5-15.name: Andrew the Hermit

5-15.bio:
The synaxarion honors Venerable Kale on May 15, recording only that she lived a life pleasing to God and reposed in peace.

Greek women bearing the name Kali may keep this day.
5-15.desc: Venerable Kale, a righteous woman remembered in the synaxarion.
5-15.name: Kale the Righteous

5-15.bio:
Silvanos had been an actor before entering the monastery of Saint Pachomios at Tabennisi, and at first kept his old frivolity. Warned by the saint that he would be expelled, he was moved to such repentance that he wept continually for the rest of his life.

Saint Pachomios later held him up as the most humble of the brethren. He is honored on the feast of his abbot.
5-15.desc: Venerable Silvanos of Tabennisi, the actor who became a model of repentance under Saint Pachomios.
5-15.name: Silvanos of Tabennisi

5-15.bio:
Panegyrios was an ascetic of Cyprus, remembered for his prayer and for the wonders worked through him, tradition placing him near the village of Malounta. Few details of his life are preserved.

He is commemorated on May 15.
5-15.desc: Venerable Panegyrios the Wonderworker of Cyprus.
5-15.name: Panegyrios of Cyprus

5-16.bio:
St. Theodore the Sanctified was the beloved disciple of St. Pachomios the Great in fourth-century Egypt. Coming to Tabennisi as a youth, he so gave himself to obedience and prayer that Pachomios loved him as a son, and after the death of his elder he guided the great communities of monks, healing divisions and strengthening the brotherhood in the common life.

He is called the Sanctified from the holiness of his life, and the Church honors him beside his teacher as a pillar of Egyptian monasticism. He is commemorated on May 16.
5-16.name: Theodore the Sanctified

5-16.bio:
Alexander studied at Alexandria under Clement and became a bishop in Cappadocia, where he was imprisoned as a confessor under Septimius Severus. Released, he went to Jerusalem and was chosen to share the see with the aged bishop Narcissus.

He founded a great library in Jerusalem and ordained Origen a priest. In the persecution of Decius he was imprisoned at Caesarea, where he died around 250.
5-16.desc: Hieromartyr Alexander, Bishop of Jerusalem, disciple of Clement of Alexandria and friend of Origen.
5-16.name: Alexander of Jerusalem

5-16.bio:
Nicholas was a learned official (mystikos) of the imperial court and disciple of Patriarch Photios before being raised to the patriarchal throne in 901. He resisted the fourth marriage of the Emperor Leo VI, was deposed for it, and later restored.

He worked for peace with Bulgaria and reposed in 925.
5-16.desc: Saint Nicholas the Mystikos, Patriarch of Constantinople, who upheld the canons against the emperor.
5-16.name: Nicholas Mystikos

5-16.bio:
The monks of the Lavra of Saint Sabbas in the Judean desert were attacked by Arab raiders seeking plunder. Finding nothing, the attackers tortured and killed many of the brethren, some by smoke in a cave.

The synaxarion honors these fathers on May 16; similar attacks are recorded in both the seventh and the eighth centuries.
5-16.desc: Holy Monastic Martyrs of the Lavra of Saint Sabbas, slain by Arab raiders.
5-16.name: Monastic Martyrs of Saint Sabbas Lavra

5-16.bio:
Makarios was born in Trikala of Corinthia in 1731 and was chosen Archbishop of Corinth in 1764. Forced from his see after the Orlov revolt, he devoted himself to the spiritual renewal of the Greek people, gathering the texts of the Philokalia with Saint Nikodemos of the Holy Mountain.

He spent his last years on Chios, preparing New Martyrs for their confession, and reposed in 1805. His principal feast is April 17.
5-16.desc: Saint Makarios Notaras, Archbishop of Corinth, father of the Kollyvades and compiler of the Philokalia.
5-16.name: Makarios Notaras of Corinth

5-16.bio:
Vukasin was a Serbian peasant from the village of Klepci in Herzegovina who was taken to the Jasenovac camp during the Second World War. Tradition relates that his executioner offered to spare him if he would praise the regime, and that Vukasin answered, Do your work, child.

He was killed in 1943 and was glorified by the Serbian Church in 1998.
5-16.desc: New Martyr Vukasin of Klepci, killed at Jasenovac for refusing to curse Christ.
5-16.name: Vukasin of Klepci

5-16.bio:
Theodore was bishop of Vrsac in the Banat and in 1594 led the Serbs of the region in an uprising against Ottoman rule. When the uprising failed he was captured and, refusing to renounce his faith, was flayed alive.

He is honored by the Serbian Church as a hieromartyr.
5-16.desc: Hieromartyr Theodore, Bishop of Vrsac, flayed alive by the Turks.
5-16.name: Theodore of Vrsac

5-17.bio:
The Holy Apostle Andronikos was one of the Seventy, greeted by St. Paul in the Epistle to the Romans as his kinsman and fellow prisoner, notable among the apostles and in Christ before him. With his fellow laborer Junia he preached the Gospel and turned many from idols to the living God.

Tradition honors him as a tireless missionary of the apostolic age whose labors bore fruit in many lands. He is commemorated on May 17.
5-17.name: Andronikos the Apostle

5-17.bio:
Junia is greeted by Saint Paul in the Epistle to the Romans, together with Andronikos, as his kinsfolk and fellow prisoners who were outstanding among the apostles and in Christ before him. Tradition relates that she labored with Andronikos in preaching the Gospel and in bringing many to baptism.

Their relics were found in Constantinople in the fifth century.
5-17.desc: Holy Apostle Junia, companion of Andronikos and kinswoman of Saint Paul.
5-17.name: Junia the Apostle

5-17.bio:
Athanasios was born in Karytaina in Arcadia in the seventeenth century and became Bishop of Christianoupolis (Triphylia) in the Peloponnese. He shepherded his flock with love under Ottoman rule and was known for wonders in his lifetime.

He reposed in 1735 and his relics are venerated in Kyparissia and Karytaina.
5-17.desc: Saint Athanasios the New, Bishop of Christianoupolis in the Peloponnese, wonderworker.
5-17.name: Athanasios of Christianoupolis

5-17.bio:
Solochon, Pamphamer and Pamphylon were Egyptian soldiers serving at Chalcedon under the Emperor Maximian. Refusing to sacrifice to idols, they were beaten and tortured; tradition relates that Solochon endured especially cruel torments and, carried to the house of a Christian, gave up his soul after instructing those present in the faith.

They are commemorated on May 17.
5-17.desc: Holy Martyrs Solochon, Pamphamer and Pamphylon, Egyptian soldiers martyred at Chalcedon.
5-17.name: Solochon, Pamphamer and Pamphylon

5-17.bio:
Nektarios and Theophanes were brothers from Ioannina who became monks and, in the sixteenth century, climbed the rock of the earlier hermit Varlaam at Meteora. There they built the Monastery of All Saints, known as Varlaam, and gathered a brotherhood.

They reposed in the 1540s and are honored as founders of one of the great monasteries of Meteora.
5-17.desc: Venerable Nektarios and Theophanes the Apsarades, brothers and founders of the Varlaam Monastery at Meteora.
5-17.name: Nektarios and Theophanes of Meteora

5-17.bio:
Nicholas was a young man from Metsovo in Epirus who, while working in Trikala, was pressured into accepting Islam. Returning home in remorse, he repented and, resolving to confess Christ, went back to Trikala.

Refusing to deny his faith a second time, he was burned alive in 1617. His relics are venerated at Meteora and in Metsovo.
5-17.desc: New Martyr Nicholas of Metsovo, burned alive at Trikala.
5-17.name: Nicholas of Metsovo

5-17.bio:
Theodoretos was a priest of Antioch who remained at his post when Julian the Apostate confiscated the treasures of the churches. Arrested and tortured for refusing to surrender the sacred vessels and to sacrifice to idols, he was beheaded in 362.

He is commemorated on May 17.
5-17.desc: Holy Martyr Theodoretos the Presbyter of Antioch, put to death under Julian the Apostate.
5-17.name: Theodoretos of Antioch

5-18.bio:
The Holy Martyr Theodotus of Ancyra suffered under the persecution of Diocletian at the beginning of the fourth century. An innkeeper by trade, he secretly aided the persecuted Christians of the city; when seven holy virgins of Ancyra were put to death for their faith, tradition tells that Theodotus recovered their bodies and gave them burial, though it was forbidden on pain of death. For this he was seized, tortured, and beheaded.

He is commemorated together with the Seven Virgins of Ancyra on May 18, a witness that mercy toward the martyrs is itself a crown.
5-18.desc: Holy Martyr Theodotus of Ancyra and the Seven Virgins.
5-18.name: Theodotus of Ancyra

5-18.bio:
Peter, a young Christian of Lampsacus on the Hellespont, refused to sacrifice to Aphrodite and was tortured and killed under the Emperor Decius. Dionysios, Andrew and Paul were arrested with him, and the virgin Christina, who encouraged them, was also martyred.

They are commemorated together on May 18.
5-18.desc: Holy Martyrs Peter, Dionysios, Andrew, Paul and Christina, who suffered at Lampsacus under Decius.
5-18.greek: Πέτρος, Διονύσιος, Ανδρέας, Παύλος και Χριστίνα
5-18.name: Martyrs of Lampsacus: Peter, Dionysios, Andrew, Paul and Christina

5-18.bio:
Tekousa, Alexandra, Claudia, Phaine, Euphrasia, Matrona and Julia were elderly Christian virgins of Ancyra in Galatia. In the persecution of Diocletian they were paraded through the city and drowned in a lake with stones about their necks.

Saint Theodotos recovered their bodies for burial and was martyred for it; they are honored together on May 18.
5-18.desc: The Seven Virgin Martyrs of Ancyra, drowned in a lake for their faith and honored with Saint Theodotos.
5-18.greek: Τεκούσα, Αλεξανδρία, Κλαυδία, Φαεινή, Ευφρασία, Ματρώνα και Ιουλία
5-18.name: Seven Virgin Martyrs of Ancyra

5-18.bio:
Stephen was the son of the Emperor Basil I and the brother of Leo VI. Educated by Patriarch Photios, he was made Patriarch of Constantinople in 886 while still very young.

He governed the Church with humility and charity for seven years and reposed in 893.
5-18.desc: Saint Stephen, Patriarch of Constantinople, brother of the Emperor Leo the Wise.
5-18.name: Stephen of Constantinople

5-18.bio:
Theodore was born in Jerusalem of Greek parents and became Pope of Rome in 642. He firmly opposed the Monothelite heresy supported by Constantinople and prepared the way for the Lateran Council under his successor Saint Martin.

He was generous to the poor and reposed in 649.
5-18.desc: Saint Theodore, Pope of Rome, defender of Orthodoxy against Monothelitism.
5-18.name: Theodore, Pope of Rome

5-18.bio:
Potamon was bishop of Heraclea in Egypt and suffered in the persecution of Maximian, losing an eye for his confession. He took part in the Council of Nicaea and later defended Saint Athanasios against the Arians.

Tradition relates that he was beaten to death by Arian agents around the year 341.
5-18.desc: Hieromartyr Potamon, Bishop of Heraclea in Egypt, confessor and father of Nicaea.
5-18.name: Potamon of Heraclea

5-18.bio:
David and Tarichan were young brothers of a noble Georgian family in the seventh century whose uncle, having embraced Islam, sought to force them to follow him and to seize their inheritance. When they refused to abandon Christ, he killed them.

They are honored by the Georgian Church as child martyrs.
5-18.desc: Holy Child Martyrs David and Tarichan of Georgia, killed by their apostate uncle.
5-18.name: David and Tarichan of Georgia

5-19.bio:
The Holy Hieromartyr Patrick was Bishop of Prusa in Bithynia in the early centuries of the Church. Brought before the pagan governor with priests of his church, he confessed Christ as the Creator of all, refusing to ascribe the works of God to the idols, and for his boldness he was put to death by the sword together with his companions.

The Church honors him among the shepherd-martyrs who taught the truth with their words and sealed it with their blood. He is commemorated on May 19.
5-19.name: Patrick, Bishop of Prusa

5-19.bio:
Memnon was an abbot of a monastery in Egypt, remembered for his gift of working wonders; tradition relates that he brought forth water in the desert and delivered the district from locusts through his prayer.

He reposed in peace and is commemorated on May 19.
5-19.desc: Venerable Memnon the Wonderworker, abbot in Egypt.
5-19.name: Memnon the Wonderworker

5-19.bio:
The synaxarion honors the holy martyr Theotime on May 19, recording that she gave her life for Christ. The circumstances of her martyrdom are not preserved.

She is commemorated together with Saint Patrick of Prusa.
5-19.name: Theotime the Martyr

5-19.bio:
The synaxarion records the martyrdom of a holy woman named Kyriaki on May 19, distinct from the Great Martyr Kyriaki of July 7. The details of her life and suffering are not preserved.

She is honored together with the other saints of the day.
5-19.desc: Holy Martyr Kyriaki, commemorated on May 19.
5-19.name: Kyriaki the Martyr

5-19.bio:
John, Konon and eleven fellow monks of the Monastery of the Theotokos at Kantara in Cyprus refused to accept the Latin teaching on unleavened bread when the island was under Frankish rule. After three years of imprisonment and beatings they were dragged through the streets of Nicosia and burned.

They suffered in 1231 and are honored by the Church of Cyprus on May 19.
5-19.desc: The Thirteen Venerable Martyrs of the Kantara Monastery in Cyprus, burned by the Latins for refusing to alter the faith.
5-19.greek: Ιωάννης, Κόνων και οι συν αυτοίς Οσιομάρτυρες της Καντάρας
5-19.name: Thirteen Monastic Martyrs of Kantara

5-19.bio:
John, nicknamed Arnaoutogiannis, was a Greek field-guard (dragatis) who, tradition relates, was falsely accused before the Turkish authorities and pressed to change his faith. Refusing, he was put to death for Christ.

He is counted among the New Martyrs of the Ottoman period and commemorated on May 19.
5-19.desc: New Martyr John the Dragatis, called Arnaoutogiannis.
5-19.name: John Arnaoutogiannis

5-2.bio:
St. Athanasios the Great was Archbishop of Alexandria in the fourth century and the foremost defender of the divinity of Christ against the Arian heresy. Present at the First Ecumenical Council of Nicaea as a young deacon, he spent the rest of his life upholding the Nicene faith, enduring five exiles rather than yield.

His writings, including On the Incarnation and the Life of St. Anthony, shaped the faith and the monasticism of the whole Church. He reposed in 373. The Church commemorates him on January 18 together with St. Cyril, and on May 2 the return of his relics.
5-2.desc: Archbishop of Alexandria, defender of the Nicene faith.
5-2.name: Athanasios of Alexandria

5-2.bio:
Hesperos and Zoe were Christian slaves of a pagan master in Attalia of Pamphylia in the second century, and raised their two sons Kyriakos and Theodoulos in the faith. When the family refused to eat food offered to idols, the master had them tortured.

All four remained firm and were finally cast into a heated furnace, where they gave up their souls. Zoe is one of the most loved women's names in the Greek calendar, and her name-day is kept on this feast.
5-2.desc: Holy Martyrs Hesperos, Zoe and their children Kyriakos and Theodoulos, a Christian slave family martyred at Attalia.
5-2.name: Hesperos and Zoe with their sons Kyriakos and Theodoulos

5-2.bio:
Matrona Nikonova was born blind in a village of the Tula region in the 1880s. From childhood she showed unusual spiritual insight, and people came to her for prayer and counsel. Later she lost the use of her legs and lived in Moscow, moving from house to house through the years of persecution.

She received the many who sought her out, urging them to prayer, the sacraments and the sign of the Cross. She reposed in 1952 and was glorified by the Russian Church in 1999; her relics rest at the Pokrovsky Monastery in Moscow.
5-2.desc: Blessed Matrona of Moscow, the blind ascetic and counselor of twentieth-century Russia.
5-2.name: Matrona of Moscow

5-2.bio:
Boris ruled Bulgaria in the ninth century and received baptism from Constantinople, taking the name Michael. He led his nobles and people into the Church, welcomed the disciples of Saints Cyril and Methodios, and fostered the Slavonic liturgy and letters.

Toward the end of his life he withdrew to a monastery, returning briefly to secure the Christian succession before ending his days as a monk in 907.
5-2.desc: Saint Boris, in baptism Michael, Prince of Bulgaria and Equal-to-the-Apostles, who brought his people to Christ.
5-2.name: Boris the Baptizer of Bulgaria

5-2.bio:
Basil was born near Moscow in the late fifteenth century and, while apprenticed to a shoemaker, took up the ascetic path of folly for Christ. He went about the city barefoot in all seasons, owning nothing and speaking hard truths to the powerful, including Tsar Ivan the Terrible, who nonetheless revered him.

He reposed in 1557 and was buried beside the Kremlin; the famous cathedral on Red Square is popularly called by his name.
5-2.desc: Blessed Basil, Fool-for-Christ of Moscow, who walked barefoot through the city and rebuked even the Tsar.
5-2.name: Basil the Blessed of Moscow

5-2.bio:
Little is recorded of Venerable Jordan beyond his name and the note that he was a monk who reposed in peace and was granted the gift of working wonders. The synaxarion honors him briefly on May 2.

Greeks who bear the name Iordanis, taken from the river of Christ's baptism, may also keep this day.
5-2.desc: Venerable Jordan the Wonderworker, an ascetic remembered in the Greek synaxarion.
5-2.name: Jordan the Wonderworker

5-20.bio:
St. Lydia of Philippi holds a beloved place in the Church as the first person baptized by the Apostle Paul on European soil. A seller of purple goods from Thyatira, she was a devout worshipper of God, and as she listened to Paul by the riverside at Philippi the Lord opened her heart to receive the Gospel. She was baptized with her whole household and welcomed the Apostles into her home.

Her hospitality made her house the first gathering place of the church at Philippi, and she is honored as Equal-to-the-Apostles in Greek tradition. She is commemorated on May 20.
5-20.desc: St. Lydia of Philippi, the first European convert of the Apostle Paul.
5-20.name: Lydia of Philippi

5-20.bio:
Thalleleos was a young physician from Lebanon who treated the sick without payment and led many to Christ. Arrested at Aegae in Cilicia under the Emperor Numerian, he was subjected to tortures which, tradition relates, turned back upon his tormentors.

He was beheaded around 284, and his companions Asterios and Alexander, converted by his witness, suffered with him. He is numbered among the Holy Unmercenaries.
5-20.desc: Holy Martyr Thalleleos the Unmercenary physician of Aegae, beheaded under Numerian.
5-20.name: Thalleleos the Unmercenary

5-20.bio:
Niketas, John and Joseph were hermits on Mount Provateion in Chios in the eleventh century. Tradition relates that they found an icon of the Theotokos hanging in a myrtle tree and, foretelling the rise of Constantine Monomachos to the throne, received from him the means to build the Nea Moni.

The monastery became one of the glories of Byzantine art, and the three founders are honored on May 20.
5-20.desc: Venerable Niketas, John and Joseph, hermits of Chios and founders of the Nea Moni.
5-20.greek: Νικήτας, Ιωάννης και Ιωσήφ της Νέας Μονής Χίου
5-20.name: Founders of Nea Moni: Niketas, John and Joseph

5-20.bio:
Thalassios was abbot of a monastery in Libya in the seventh century and a correspondent of Saint Maximos the Confessor, who dedicated several works to him. His own Four Centuries on love, self-control and the life of the mind are included in the Philokalia.

He reposed in peace around 660.
5-20.desc: Venerable Thalassios of Libya, abbot and spiritual writer, friend of Saint Maximos the Confessor.
5-20.name: Thalassios the Libyan

5-20.bio:
Alexander and Asterios were among the executioners of Saint Thalleleos at Aegae who, seeing the wonders that accompanied his torments, confessed Christ themselves.

They were beheaded with him and are commemorated on the same day.
5-20.desc: Holy Martyrs Alexander and Asterios, converted by Saint Thalleleos and martyred with him.
5-20.name: Alexander and Asterios

5-20.bio:
In 1087 sailors from Bari carried the relics of Saint Nicholas from Myra in Lycia, then under Turkish threat, to their own city, where a great basilica was raised over them. The relics have continued to exude a fragrant liquid, the manna of Saint Nicholas.

The Greek calendar keeps the memory of the translation on May 20.
5-20.desc: Commemoration of the translation of the relics of Saint Nicholas from Myra to Bari.
5-20.name: Translation of the Relics of Nicholas to Bari

5-20.bio:
Zabulon, a Cappadocian nobleman related to Saint George, and his wife Sosanna, sister of the Patriarch of Jerusalem, were the parents of Saint Nina. Tradition relates that they gave themselves to the service of God, Zabulon in the wilderness of the Jordan and Sosanna in caring for the poor in Jerusalem.

The Georgian Church honors them on May 20.
5-20.desc: Righteous Zabulon and Sosanna, parents of Saint Nina, Enlightener of Georgia.
5-20.name: Zabulon and Sosanna

5-21.bio:
St. Constantine the Great, Equal-to-the-Apostles, was the first Roman Emperor to embrace Christianity. After his vision of the Cross and his victory under its sign, he ended the persecutions with the Edict of Milan, convened the First Ecumenical Council at Nicaea, and founded Constantinople as a Christian capital. His mother, St. Helen, traveled in old age to the Holy Land, where according to tradition she found the Precious Cross of the Lord and built churches on the holy sites.

Mother and son are commemorated together on May 21, one of the great name days of the Greek world, honored as Equals-to-the-Apostles for turning an empire toward Christ.
5-21.desc: Equal-to-the-Apostles Emperor Constantine the Great and his mother Helen.
5-21.name: Constantine and Helen

5-21.bio:
Pachomios was born in Little Russia, captured by the Tatars and sold to a Turk in Ousaki in Asia Minor, where he served for many years without abandoning his faith. Freed, he became a monk on Mount Athos under the elder Joseph.

Returning to Ousaki, he was accused of having once accepted Islam and, refusing to deny Christ, was beheaded in 1730.
5-21.desc: Venerable Martyr Pachomios of Ousaki, an Athonite monk beheaded for Christ.
5-21.name: Pachomios the New Martyr

5-21.bio:
Kassianos was a Greek nobleman named Constantine who came to Moscow in the entourage of Sophia Palaiologina. He became a monk at the Ferapontov Monastery and later founded a monastery near Uglich on the Volga.

He reposed in 1504 and is honored as a wonderworker by the Russian Church.
5-21.desc: Venerable Kassianos the Greek, wonderworker of Uglich.
5-21.name: Kassianos the Greek

5-21.bio:
Constantine was a prince of Kievan Rus who in the twelfth century was sent to rule Murom, then still largely pagan. His son Michael was killed by the pagans, and tradition relates that his patience and the wonders of an icon of the Theotokos won the people to baptism.

He reposed in 1129 with his sons and is honored with them on the feast of his namesake, Constantine the Great.
5-21.desc: Holy Princes Constantine, Michael and Theodore of Murom, enlighteners of that region.
5-21.name: Constantine of Murom with his sons Michael and Theodore

5-21.bio:
Christopher was a Christian official who was chosen Patriarch of Antioch in the tenth century while the city was under Muslim rule. He was respected for his justice and his care for the Christians of the region.

He was murdered in 967 by those who resented his defense of his flock and is honored as a hieromartyr.
5-21.desc: Hieromartyr Christopher I, Patriarch of Antioch, murdered for his faith.
5-21.name: Christopher of Antioch

5-21.bio:
Timothy, Polios and Eutychios were deacons in the Roman province of Mauretania who preached Christ and were put to death for their faith. Few details of their martyrdom have been preserved.

They are commemorated on May 21.
5-21.desc: Holy Martyrs Timothy, Polios and Eutychios, deacons of Africa.
5-21.name: Timothy, Polios and Eutychios

5-22.bio:
The Holy Martyr Basiliskos suffered for Christ in Pontus at the beginning of the fourth century, during the persecutions of the pagan emperors. Tradition remembers him as a kinsman of the Great Martyr Theodore the Recruit and a soldier like him. Refusing to sacrifice to the idols, he endured imprisonment and cruel treatment, and was beheaded at Comana, faithful to the end.

The Church honors in him the courage of the soldier-martyrs who counted loyalty to Christ above life itself. He is commemorated on May 22.
5-22.name: Basiliskos

5-22.bio:
The Second Ecumenical Council was convened at Constantinople in 381 under the Emperor Theodosius the Great. Led by Saints Meletios of Antioch, Gregory the Theologian and Gregory of Nyssa, the Fathers condemned the heresy of Macedonius against the Holy Spirit and completed the Creed.

The Church keeps their memory on May 22.
5-22.desc: Commemoration of the Holy Fathers of the Second Ecumenical Council at Constantinople.
5-22.name: Fathers of the Second Ecumenical Council

5-22.bio:
Paul was born in Sopoto of Arcadia and, having once denied Christ under duress, repented and became a monk on Mount Athos. Prepared for confession by the fathers of the Holy Mountain, he returned to the Peloponnese.

He confessed Christ before the pasha of Tripolis and was beheaded in 1818.
5-22.desc: Venerable Martyr Paul of Aroania, an Athonite monk beheaded at Tripolis.
5-22.name: Paul the Peloponnesian

5-22.bio:
The synaxarion honors Venerable Sophia the Physician on May 22, recording that she practiced medicine among the poor without payment and lived a life of prayer and mercy. The details of her life are not otherwise preserved.

She is distinct from the Martyr Sophia of September 17.
5-22.desc: Venerable Sophia the Physician, who healed the sick and served the poor.
5-22.name: Sophia the Physician

5-22.bio:
John Vladimir ruled the Serbian land of Zeta (Duklja) at the turn of the eleventh century and was known for his piety and justice. Captured by Tsar Samuel of Bulgaria, he married the Tsar's daughter Kosara and was restored to his throne.

He was treacherously beheaded in 1016 by Samuel's successor. His relics are venerated near Elbasan in Albania and he is honored throughout the Balkans.
5-22.desc: Holy King John Vladimir of Serbia, wonderworker, beheaded by treachery.
5-22.name: John Vladimir of Serbia

5-22.bio:
The synaxarion honors the martyr Markellos on May 22, recording only that he gave his life for Christ. The place of his martyrdom is not preserved.

He is commemorated together with Saint Basiliskos.
5-22.name: Markellos the Martyr

5-22.bio:
Zacharias was a priest of Prousa in Asia Minor who, in a moment of weakness, had embraced Islam. Repenting, he confessed his return to Christ before the judge and refused every inducement to recant.

He was beheaded in 1802.
5-22.desc: Hieromartyr Zacharias the New of Prousa, a priest beheaded for returning to Christ.
5-22.name: Zacharias of Prousa

5-23.bio:
St. Michael the Confessor was Bishop of Synnada in Phrygia in the eighth and ninth centuries. A man of holy life, he served the Church in times of trouble and stood firm for the veneration of the holy icons when the iconoclast emperors sought to destroy them. For his confession he was driven from his see and endured exile and hardship until his repose.

The Church names him Confessor because he suffered for the truth without denying it, and honors him among the defenders of the icons. He is commemorated on May 23.
5-23.name: Michael the Confessor

5-23.bio:
Mary of Clopas stood with the Theotokos and Mary Magdalene at the Cross of Christ, as the Gospel of John records, and was among the women who came to the tomb with spices on the morning of the Resurrection. Tradition relates that she was the wife of Clopas, brother of Joseph the Betrothed.

She is honored among the Myrrhbearers on May 23.
5-23.desc: Saint Mary the wife of Clopas, one of the Myrrhbearing Women.
5-23.name: Mary of Clopas

5-23.bio:
Eumenios Saridakis was born in Crete in 1931 and became a monk as a youth. Contracting leprosy, he was sent to the hospital for infectious diseases in Athens, where, after his healing, he chose to remain for the rest of his life as priest and comforter of the sick.

He was known for his humility, ceaseless prayer and gift of consolation. He reposed in 1999 and was glorified by the Ecumenical Patriarchate in 2020.
5-23.desc: Venerable Eumenios the New (Saridakis), the God-bearing elder of the leper colony of Athens.
5-23.name: Eumenios of Crete

5-23.bio:
Joachim was born on Ithaca in 1786 and became a monk on Mount Athos. Returning to his island, he lived in great simplicity, comforting the poor and healing the sick, so that the people called him Papoulakis, the little father.

He reposed in 1868, and his relics were found incorrupt; this day commemorates their translation, while his principal feast is March 2.
5-23.desc: Venerable Joachim of Ithaca, called Papoulakis, ascetic and wonderworker of the Ionian Islands.
5-23.name: Joachim of Ithaca

5-23.bio:
Euphrosyne was a princess of Polotsk who refused marriage and became a nun in her youth. She founded a convent and a monastery in Polotsk, copied books, and encouraged learning among her people.

Toward the end of her life she went on pilgrimage to Jerusalem, where she reposed in 1173.
5-23.desc: Venerable Euphrosyne of Polotsk, princess and abbess.
5-23.name: Euphrosyne of Polotsk

5-23.bio:
The synaxarion honors the martyr Salonas the Roman on May 23, recording that he died for Christ. Further details are not preserved.

He is commemorated together with Saint Michael of Synnada.
5-23.name: Salonas the Roman

5-23.bio:
Manaen is named in the Acts of the Apostles among the prophets and teachers of the Church at Antioch, together with Barnabas and Saul, and is described as having been brought up with Herod the Tetrarch. It was through these prophets that Barnabas and Paul were set apart for their first missionary journey.

Tradition relates that he preached the Gospel and reposed in peace.
5-23.desc: Saint Manaen, prophet and teacher of the Church of Antioch, named in the Acts of the Apostles.
5-23.name: Manaen the Prophet

5-24.bio:
St. Symeon the Stylite of the Wonderful Mountain lived in the sixth century near Antioch. Drawn to asceticism from childhood, he took up the rare and severe podvig of the pillar saints, dwelling on a column in fasting, vigil, and unceasing prayer for the greater part of his long life, after the pattern of the first Symeon the Stylite.

From his pillar he taught, counseled, and healed the many who came to him, and was revered as a wonderworker. He is commemorated on May 24.
5-24.desc: Venerable Symeon the Stylite of the Younger.
5-24.name: Symeon Stylites

5-24.bio:
Kyriakos was an ascetic of the village of Evrychou in the Troodos region of Cyprus, honored locally as a wonderworker. His church in Evrychou preserves his memory and his relics.

Few details of his life have been preserved; he is commemorated on May 24.
5-24.desc: Venerable Kyriakos the Wonderworker of Evrychou in Cyprus.
5-24.name: Kyriakos of Evrychou

5-24.bio:
Meletios was a Roman general in Galatia who, tradition relates, destroyed the pagan temples of the region and was denounced to the Emperor Antoninus. He was tortured and put to death together with a great multitude of his soldiers and their families who had believed through him.

Among those named with him are John, Stephen, Serapion and Kallinikos. They are commemorated on May 24.
5-24.desc: Holy Martyr Meletios the General and the many soldiers who suffered with him in Galatia.
5-24.name: Meletios the General and Companions

5-24.bio:
Niketas was a tax collector of Pereslavl who oppressed the poor until, struck by the words of the Prophet Isaiah at church, he repented. He became a monk, wearing heavy chains and standing on a pillar in prayer.

He healed many, including the young prince Michael of Chernigov, and was killed in 1186 by robbers who thought his chains were silver.
5-24.desc: Venerable Niketas the Stylite, wonderworker of Pereslavl-Zalessky.
5-24.name: Niketas the Stylite of Pereslavl

5-24.bio:
Agatharchos is honored as an early bishop of the island of Leukas in the Ionian Sea, tradition placing him in the fourth century. He is commemorated together with the Five God-bearing Fathers who are venerated as ascetics of the island.

His feast is kept locally on May 24.
5-24.desc: Saint Agatharchos, Bishop of Leukas, honored with the Five God-bearing Fathers of the island.
5-24.name: Agatharchos of Leukas

5-25.bio:
The Church commemorates on May 25 the Third Finding of the honorable head of St. John the Forerunner. According to tradition, the relic had been hidden during the years of iconoclasm; when the veneration of holy things was restored, the head of the Baptist was revealed once more and brought with honor to Constantinople, received by emperor and patriarch amid great rejoicing.

Each finding of the precious head renewed the devotion of the faithful to the Forerunner, the greatest of the prophets and the first preacher of repentance. The feast bears witness to the care of God in preserving the relics of His saints.
5-25.desc: Third Finding of the Precious Head of John the Baptist.
5-25.name: Third Finding of the Head of John the Baptist

5-25.bio:
The synaxarion honors the martyr Celestine on May 25, recording that he died for Christ. Further details of his life are not preserved.

He is commemorated together with the Third Finding of the Head of the Forerunner.
5-25.name: Celestine the Martyr

5-25.bio:
The synaxarion records Venerable Olbianos as a monk who lived in asceticism and reposed in peace. He is distinct from the hieromartyr Olbianos of Aneai.

He is commemorated on May 25.
5-25.desc: Venerable Olbianos, an ascetic who reposed in peace.
5-25.name: Olbianos the Venerable

5-25.bio:
Dionysios became Bishop of Milan in 351 and at the council held there in 355 refused to condemn Saint Athanasios at the demand of the Arian emperor Constantius. For this he was exiled to Cappadocia, where he died around 360.

His relics were later returned to Milan through the care of Saint Basil the Great and Saint Ambrose.
5-25.desc: Saint Dionysios, Bishop of Milan, confessor exiled by the Arians.
5-25.name: Dionysios of Milan

5-25.bio:
Innocent Borisov was born in 1800 and became one of the most celebrated preachers and theologians of the Russian Church, teaching at Kiev and serving as Archbishop of Kherson and Taurida. During the Crimean War he ministered fearlessly in besieged Sevastopol and Odessa.

He reposed in 1857 and was glorified in 1997.
5-25.desc: Saint Innocent, Archbishop of Kherson, preacher and defender of Odessa.
5-25.name: Innocent of Kherson

5-25.bio:
Zenobios was born in Florence to a noble family and was brought to Christ by his teacher. Ordained by the bishop of Florence, he became a friend of Saint Ambrose of Milan and later Bishop of Florence himself.

He was renowned for wonders in his lifetime and reposed in the early fifth century.
5-25.desc: Saint Zenobios, Bishop of Florence, friend of Saint Ambrose.
5-25.name: Zenobios of Florence

5-26.bio:
The Holy Apostle Karpos was one of the Seventy, a companion and fellow laborer of St. Paul. The Apostle mentions him in his second letter to Timothy, recalling the cloak and books he had left with Karpos at Troas. Tradition holds that he served the Church as a bishop and gave himself wholly to the preaching of the Gospel.

The Church honors him among the apostolic men through whom the faith was planted in the first generation. He is commemorated on May 26.
5-26.name: Karpos the Apostle

5-26.bio:
Alphaeus is named in the Gospels as the father of the Apostle James the Less and, according to tradition, of the Evangelist Matthew. Tradition relates that he preached the Gospel and reposed in peace.

He is commemorated with the Apostle Karpos on May 26.
5-26.desc: Holy Apostle Alphaeus, father of the Apostles James and Matthew.
5-26.name: Alphaeus the Apostle

5-26.bio:
Alexander was born in Thessalonica and as a young man embraced Islam, becoming a wandering dervish. Repenting, he returned to Christ and travelled to Smyrna, where he openly declared his faith before the judge.

He was beheaded in 1794.
5-26.desc: New Martyr Alexander of Thessalonica, the former dervish, beheaded at Smyrna.
5-26.name: Alexander the Dervish

5-26.bio:
Synesios was bishop of Karpasia in the north-east of Cyprus, honored on the island as a wonderworker. Tradition places him in the early Christian centuries; his church at Rizokarpaso preserves his memory.

He is commemorated on May 26.
5-26.desc: Saint Synesios, Bishop of Karpasia in Cyprus, wonderworker.
5-26.name: Synesios of Karpasia

5-26.bio:
Tradition relates that Averkios and his sister Helen were children of the Apostle Alphaeus. Averkios was tied naked among bees and died of their stings for confessing Christ.

He is commemorated with his father and sister on May 26.
5-26.desc: Holy Martyr Averkios, brother of the Martyr Helen and child of the Apostle Alphaeus.
5-26.name: Averkios the Martyr

5-26.bio:
Helen, sister of the martyr Averkios and, according to tradition, daughter of the Apostle Alphaeus, was stoned to death for confessing Christ.

She is commemorated with her family on May 26.
5-26.desc: Holy Martyr Helen, daughter of the Apostle Alphaeus, stoned for her faith.
5-26.name: Helen the Martyr

5-26.bio:
George was a young Bulgarian from Sofia, a goldsmith by trade, who was pressed by the Turks to embrace Islam. Refusing, he confessed Christ and was burned alive.

He suffered in the early sixteenth century and is honored by the Bulgarian Church.
5-26.desc: New Martyr George of Sofia, burned for refusing Islam.
5-26.name: George the New Martyr of Bulgaria

5-27.bio:
St. John the Russian was a soldier taken captive during the wars between Russia and the Ottoman Empire early in the eighteenth century, and sold into slavery in Prokopi of Asia Minor. Refusing to abandon his faith, he served his master humbly, living in a stable in prayer and fasting, and came to be revered even by his captors as a man of God.

He reposed in 1730, and his incorrupt relics were brought with the Asia Minor refugees in 1924 to New Prokopi on the island of Evia, where his shrine is one of the great pilgrimage centers of Greece. His feast is May 27.
5-27.desc: St. John the Russian, Confessor, of Evia.
5-27.name: John the Russian

5-27.bio:
Therapon was bishop of Sardis in Lydia and brought many pagans to Christ. During the persecution of Valerian he was arrested, dragged in chains through the cities of Asia and, tradition relates, bound to a dry stake which afterward put forth leaves.

He was beheaded around 259. His name-day is widely kept on this date.
5-27.desc: Hieromartyr Therapon, Bishop of Sardis, beheaded under Valerian.
5-27.name: Therapon of Sardis

5-27.bio:
The synaxarion honors the martyr Alypios on May 27, recording that he was put to death for Christ. Further details are not preserved.

He is commemorated together with Saint John the Russian.
5-27.name: Alypios the Martyr

5-27.bio:
Julius had served twenty-seven years in the Roman army with distinction when, during the persecution of Diocletian, he was denounced as a Christian at Durostorum on the Danube. Refusing to sacrifice, he told the governor that he would not betray the faith he had kept all his life.

He was beheaded around 304.
5-27.desc: Holy Martyr Julius the Veteran, a Roman soldier beheaded at Durostorum.
5-27.name: Julius the Veteran

5-27.bio:
Bede entered the monastery of Wearmouth-Jarrow in Northumbria as a child in the seventh century and spent his whole life there in prayer, study and teaching. His Ecclesiastical History of the English People is the chief source for the early Church in Britain.

He reposed in 735 while dictating a translation of the Gospel of John.
5-27.desc: Venerable Bede of Jarrow, monk, teacher and historian of the English Church.
5-27.name: Bede the Venerable

5-27.bio:
Therapon was a companion of Saint Kirill of White Lake and, in the late fourteenth century, founded a monastery near Lake Beloe that came to bear his name and was later adorned with the frescoes of Dionisy.

He went on to found another monastery near Mozhaisk and reposed in 1426.
5-27.desc: Venerable Therapon of Belozersk, founder of the Ferapontov Monastery.
5-27.name: Therapon of White Lake

5-28.bio:
The Holy Hieromartyr Helladios was a bishop of the East in the early centuries of the Church who suffered for Christ in a time of persecution. The synaxaria preserve little of his life beyond his faithful service at the altar and his steadfast confession, for which he endured torments and gave his life for the Lord.

The Church keeps his memory among the hieromartyrs, shepherds who laid down their lives for the flock after the example of the Chief Shepherd. He is commemorated on May 28.
5-28.name: Helladios

5-28.bio:
Eutyches was a bishop of Melitene in Armenia in the apostolic age, remembered as a fellow-laborer of the holy Apostles. He suffered persecution for the Gospel and was put to death.

He is commemorated on May 28.
5-28.desc: Hieromartyr Eutyches, Bishop of Melitene, co-worker of the Apostles.
5-28.name: Eutyches of Melitene

5-28.bio:
Heliconis was a Christian woman of Thessalonica who went to Corinth during the persecution of Gordian and Philip and openly rebuked the worship of idols. After cruel tortures, tradition relates, she entered the temple and cast down the statues of the gods.

She was beheaded around the year 244.
5-28.desc: Holy Martyr Heliconis of Thessalonica, beheaded at Corinth.
5-28.name: Heliconis of Thessalonica

5-28.bio:
Andrew was a Scythian slave in Constantinople in the tenth century who, called by a vision, took up the life of folly for Christ, living in the streets in rags and enduring mockery while secretly praying through the night. He was granted many visions and the gift of insight.

With his disciple Epiphanios he saw the Theotokos spreading her veil over the people in the church at Blachernae, the vision commemorated at the feast of the Protection.
5-28.desc: Venerable Andrew the Fool-for-Christ of Constantinople, who beheld the Protection of the Theotokos.
5-28.name: Andrew the Fool-for-Christ

5-28.bio:
Niketas was chosen bishop of Chalcedon in the eighth century and was known for his charity to the poor and the stranger. In the Iconoclast persecution he defended the veneration of icons and endured exile and hardship.

He reposed in peace and is honored as a confessor.
5-28.desc: Saint Niketas the Confessor, Archbishop of Chalcedon, who suffered for the holy icons.
5-28.name: Niketas of Chalcedon

5-28.bio:
Kreskes, Paul and Dioskorides were Christians of Rome who were burned alive for their confession of Christ, tradition placing their martyrdom in the third century.

They are commemorated on May 28.
5-28.desc: Holy Martyrs Kreskes, Paul and Dioskorides of Rome, burned for their faith.
5-28.name: Kreskes, Paul and Dioskorides

5-28.bio:
Mitros, a form of the name Demetrios, was a young Christian of the Peloponnese who, tradition relates, was falsely accused and pressured to accept Islam by the Turks of Tripolis. Refusing, he was put to death for Christ in 1794.

He is honored among the New Martyrs of the Peloponnese.
5-28.desc: New Martyr Mitros (Demetrios) of Tripolis in the Peloponnese.
5-28.name: Mitros of Tripolis

5-29.bio:
St. Theodosia was a nun of Constantinople who suffered in the eighth century, at the outbreak of the iconoclast persecution. When the emperor commanded the destruction of the revered icon of Christ above the Chalke Gate of the palace, tradition tells that Theodosia was among the faithful who rose to defend it, and for this she was seized and put to death, sealing her love for Christ with martyrdom.

She was long venerated in Constantinople as a protectress of the city and a helper of the sick. She is commemorated on May 29.
5-29.name: Theodosia of Constantinople

5-29.bio:
Theodosia was a young Christian of Tyre who, visiting Caesarea in Palestine, went to comfort the confessors awaiting judgment. Arrested herself, she refused to sacrifice and was tortured and cast into the sea.

She suffered around the year 308 during the persecution of Diocletian and Maximian.
5-29.desc: Virgin Martyr Theodosia of Tyre, drowned at Caesarea for her faith.
5-29.name: Theodosia of Tyre

5-29.bio:
Alexander became Patriarch of Alexandria in 313 and was the first to expose and condemn the heresy of his priest Arius, who denied the divinity of the Son. He took part in the Council of Nicaea in 325 with his deacon Athanasios, who succeeded him.

He reposed in 328.
5-29.desc: Saint Alexander, Patriarch of Alexandria, who first condemned Arius.
5-29.name: Alexander of Alexandria

5-29.bio:
Helen Dragas, a Serbian princess, married the Emperor Manuel II Palaiologos and was the mother of the last two emperors, John VIII and Constantine XI. After her husband's death she became a nun with the name Hypomone, meaning patience, and devoted herself to prayer and charity.

She reposed in 1450, three years before the fall of the City, and her relics are venerated at the Monastery of Saint Patapios near Loutraki.
5-29.desc: Venerable Hypomone, the Empress Helen Dragas, mother of the last Emperor of Constantinople.
5-29.name: Hypomone the Righteous

5-29.bio:
On Tuesday, May 29, 1453, after a siege of nearly two months, the armies of Sultan Mehmet II broke through the walls of Constantinople. The Emperor Constantine XI Palaiologos fell fighting at the gate, and the Great Church of Hagia Sophia was taken.

The Church of Greece keeps the day as a memorial of the Queen of Cities and of those who died in her defense.
5-29.desc: Memorial of the fall of Constantinople to the Ottoman Turks in 1453.
5-29.name: Fall of Constantinople

5-29.bio:
John Nannos was a young man from Thessalonica who worked in Smyrna, where he was tricked into accepting Islam. Overcome with remorse, he confessed his return to Christ before the judge.

He was beheaded in Smyrna in 1802.
5-29.desc: New Martyr John Nannos of Thessalonica, beheaded at Smyrna.
5-29.name: John Nannos of Thessalonica

5-29.bio:
Andreas Argentis was a Christian of Chios who, tradition relates, was accused of insulting Islam while in Constantinople and, refusing to convert to save his life, was beheaded in 1465.

He is honored among the early New Martyrs of the Ottoman period.
5-29.desc: New Martyr Andreas Argentis of Chios, beheaded in Constantinople.
5-29.name: Andreas Argentis

5-3.bio:
The Holy Martyrs Timothy and Maura were a young Christian couple of Egypt who suffered during the persecution of Diocletian at the end of the third century. Timothy was a reader of the Church, entrusted with the sacred books; only days after their marriage the two were arrested when he refused to surrender them. Together they endured cruel tortures and were crucified, encouraging one another in the faith to the end.

Their witness is a treasured image of married love made perfect in Christ, two lives offered together rather than parted from the Lord. They are commemorated on May 3.
5-3.desc: Holy Martyrs Timothy and Maura of Egypt.
5-3.name: Timothy and Maura

5-3.bio:
St. Peter, Bishop of Argos, was a monk of deep humility who lived in the ninth and tenth centuries. Long refusing episcopal office, he was at last persuaded to shepherd the Church of Argos in the Peloponnese, where he became a father to his flock, feeding the hungry in time of famine, ransoming captives, and caring for orphans and the poor.

He was revered even in his lifetime as a wonderworker, and after his repose his relics became a source of healing. He remains a beloved saint of the Peloponnese, commemorated on May 3.
5-3.name: Peter of Argos

5-3.bio:
Xenia was born in the late third century in the region of Kalamata to Christian parents of Italian origin. When she refused the advances of the local governor and would not sacrifice to idols, she was subjected to cruel tortures and finally beheaded.

She is honored as the patron of Kalamata, where her memory is kept with special solemnity.
5-3.desc: Great Martyr Xenia of Kalamata, virgin martyr of the Peloponnese under Diocletian.
5-3.name: Xenia of Kalamata

5-3.bio:
Theodosius was born near Kiev in the eleventh century and, against his mother's wishes, sought out Saint Anthony in his cave above the Dnieper. He became the second abbot of the community and gave it the coenobitic rule of the Studion, building the first great monastery of Rus.

He was known for humility, tireless labor and boldness before princes. He reposed in 1074, and his relics were later found incorrupt.
5-3.desc: Venerable Theodosius, abbot of the Kiev Caves Lavra and father of Russian coenobitic monasticism.
5-3.name: Theodosius of the Kiev Caves

5-3.bio:
Oikoumenios was bishop of Trikka (modern Trikala) in Thessaly, traditionally placed around the tenth century. He was a learned interpreter of Scripture, and commentaries on the Apocalypse and the Epistles have circulated under his name.

He is venerated as a wonderworker and remains a patron of the city of Trikala.
5-3.desc: Saint Oikoumenios the Wonderworker, Bishop of Trikka in Thessaly.
5-3.name: Oikoumenios of Trikka

5-3.bio:
Diodoros and the deacon Rhodopianos preached Christ in the city of Aphrodisias in Caria during the persecution of Diocletian. Seized by the pagans of the city, they were stoned to death for their confession.

The synaxarion honors them together on May 3.
5-3.desc: Holy Martyrs Diodoros and Rhodopianos the Deacon, stoned at Aphrodisias in Caria.
5-3.name: Diodoros and Rhodopianos

5-3.bio:
Theophanes was a monk of the Great Lavra on Mount Athos, where he was formed in the hesychast tradition. In the fourteenth century he was chosen Metropolitan of Peritheorion in Thrace and served his flock with pastoral care during troubled times.

He reposed in peace and is counted among the Athonite fathers.
5-3.desc: Saint Theophanes, Metropolitan of Peritheorion in Thrace, an Athonite monk and bishop of the fourteenth century.
5-3.name: Theophanes of Peritheorion

5-30.bio:
St. Isaac the Syrian lived in the seventh century. A monk from his youth, he was consecrated Bishop of Nineveh, but after only a short time he laid aside the episcopate and withdrew into the desert, giving himself wholly to stillness, prayer, and the study of the Scriptures until blindness and old age overtook him.

His Ascetical Homilies, born of that hidden life, speak of the mercy of God and the humble heart with a depth that has nourished monks and laity alike for centuries. He is commemorated on May 30.
5-30.desc: Venerable Isaac the Syrian, Bishop of Nineveh.
5-30.name: Isaac the Syrian

5-30.bio:
Emmelia was born in Cappadocia to a Christian family that had suffered in the persecutions and married Basil the Elder, a rhetorician. Of their ten children, four are numbered among the saints: Basil the Great, Gregory of Nyssa, Peter of Sebaste and Makrina the Younger.

After her husband's death she lived in prayer with her daughter Makrina on their estate at Annesi and reposed around 375. Greek women named Aimilia keep their name-day on her feast.
5-30.desc: Righteous Emmelia, mother of Saints Basil the Great, Gregory of Nyssa, Peter of Sebaste and Makrina.
5-30.name: Emmelia, Mother of Basil the Great

5-30.bio:
The synaxarion honors Venerable Barlaam on May 30, recording that he lived a life of asceticism and reposed in peace. He is distinct from the Martyr Barlaam of Antioch honored in November.

He is commemorated with the other saints of the day.
5-30.desc: Venerable Barlaam, an ascetic who reposed in peace.
5-30.name: Barlaam the Venerable

5-30.bio:
The synaxarion honors the martyr Natalios on May 30, recording that he was put to death for Christ. Further details of his life are not preserved.

He is commemorated together with Saint Isaakios of the Dalmatou Monastery.
5-30.name: Natalios the Martyr

5-30.bio:
Romanos, Teletios and Christina were Christians of Nicomedia who were put to death together with a great multitude of believers during the persecutions of the early fourth century.

They are commemorated on May 30.
5-30.desc: Holy Martyrs Romanos, Teletios and Christina and the multitude who suffered with them at Nicomedia.
5-30.name: Romanos, Teletios and Christina of Nicomedia

5-30.bio:
The synaxarion honors the martyr Euplos on May 30, recording that he was put to death for Christ. He is commemorated apart from the deacon Euplos of Catania honored in August.

Further details are not preserved.
5-30.desc: Holy Martyr Euplos, commemorated on May 30.
5-30.name: Euplos the Martyr

5-31.bio:
The Holy Martyr Hermias was an aged soldier who suffered for Christ at Comana in the second century. Summoned in his old age to sacrifice to the idols, the veteran refused, confessing the Lord whom he had served all his life, and he endured many torments with a young man's courage before being put to death by the sword.

The Church honors in him the crown of a long life made perfect in martyrdom, and in Greece his feast is kept as the name day of those called Ermis. He is commemorated on May 31.
5-31.name: Hermias the Martyr

5-31.bio:
Eusebios and Charalambos were Christians who confessed Christ during the persecutions and, according to the synaxarion, were put to death by fire. The place of their martyrdom is not preserved.

They are commemorated on May 31 together with the Martyr Hermias.
5-31.desc: Holy Martyrs Eusebios and Charalambos, burned for their faith.
5-31.name: Eusebios and Charalambos

5-31.bio:
Eustathios was a priest of the imperial palace who was raised to the patriarchal throne of Constantinople in 1019. He governed the Church for six years with prudence and reposed in peace in 1025.

He is commemorated on May 31.
5-31.name: Eustathios of Constantinople

5-31.bio:
Petronilla was a Christian virgin of Rome in the first century, buried in the catacomb of Domitilla, whom tradition calls the daughter of the Apostle Peter, in the sense that she was brought to faith by him. Tradition relates that she refused a pagan suitor and died after fasting and prayer.

Her memory has been honored in Rome since the earliest centuries.
5-31.desc: Saint Petronilla, virgin of Rome, honored as a spiritual daughter of the Apostle Peter.
5-31.name: Petronilla of Rome

5-31.bio:
Five Christians were put to death for their faith at Ascalon on the coast of Palestine, according to the synaxarion by being buried alive in the ground. Their names are not preserved.

They are commemorated on May 31.
5-31.desc: The Five Holy Martyrs who suffered at Ascalon in Palestine.
5-31.name: Five Martyrs of Ascalon

5-31.bio:
The Apostle Paul closes many of his letters by greeting those who labored with him in the Gospel: Priscilla and Aquila, Epainetos, Urbanus, Apelles, Tryphaina and Tryphosa, Persis, Epaphras, Onesiphoros and many others. The Church honors them together as the first fellow-workers in the spread of the faith.

Their synaxis is kept on May 31.
5-31.desc: Synaxis of the holy men and women named as fellow-laborers of the Apostle Paul in his epistles.
5-31.name: Co-workers of the Apostle Paul

5-31.bio:
Hierotheos was a priest of the Ottoman period who, tradition relates, was put to death for refusing to abandon the Christian faith. Few details of his life have been preserved.

He is honored among the New Martyrs on May 31.
5-31.desc: Hieromartyr Hierotheos the New, who suffered under the Turks.
5-31.name: Hierotheos the New

5-4.bio:
The Holy Martyr Pelagia was a young Christian woman of the early Church who suffered during the persecutions of the pagan emperors. Refusing to deny Christ or to be turned from her purity, she gave her life rather than betray her Lord, and the synaxaria honor her steadfast confession.

Her name, which means 'of the sea', has been borne with love by generations of Orthodox women in her memory. She is commemorated on May 4.
5-4.name: Pelagia

5-4.bio:
Nikephoros was of Italian birth and, having embraced Orthodoxy, became a monk on Mount Athos in the thirteenth century. He lived in stillness in the wilder parts of the Mountain and wrote a treatise on watchfulness and the prayer of the heart.

He was a guide to Saint Gregory Palamas, who defended his teaching, and he reposed before the year 1300.
5-4.desc: Venerable Nikephoros the Hesychast of Mount Athos, teacher of Saint Gregory Palamas.
5-4.name: Nikephoros of Mount Athos

5-4.bio:
Monica was born in North Africa in the fourth century to a Christian family and was given in marriage to a pagan husband, whom she eventually won to the faith by patience. She wept and prayed for many years for her gifted but wayward son Augustine.

She followed him to Milan, saw him baptized by Saint Ambrose, and died at Ostia in 387 while they were returning to Africa, saying she had nothing more to hope for in this life.
5-4.desc: Saint Monica, whose years of prayer and tears brought her son Augustine to Christ.
5-4.name: Monica, Mother of Augustine

5-4.bio:
Aphrodisios, together with Leontios, Antoninos, Valerian, Makrobios, Misdas and others, confessed Christ at Scythopolis in Palestine. Refusing every inducement to sacrifice, they were tortured and put to death.

The synaxarion honors the whole company on May 4.
5-4.desc: Holy Martyrs Aphrodisios, Leontios, Antoninos and their companions, who suffered at Scythopolis in Palestine.
5-4.name: Aphrodisios and Companions

5-4.bio:
Athanasios was a monk who was raised to the see of Corinth, traditionally placed in the tenth century. He governed the church of Corinth with gentleness and kept his monastic discipline as a bishop.

He reposed in peace and is remembered in the Greek synaxarion on May 4.
5-4.desc: Venerable Athanasios, Bishop of Corinth, an ascetic hierarch of the Byzantine period.
5-4.name: Athanasios of Corinth

5-4.bio:
Florian was an officer of the Roman army in the province of Noricum. During the persecution of Diocletian he openly declared himself a Christian when the governor sought out believers, and after scourging he was thrown into the river Enns with a stone tied to his neck, around the year 304.
